content.title: Derivatives of Inverse Functions
content.overview: This lesson covers the relationship between the derivative of a function and the derivative of its inverse. It focuses on the 'Swap and Reciprocal' strategy to calculate the rate of change of an inverse function at a specific point, ensuring mathematical justification and correct unit conversion.
learning_objectives: Identify the corresponding input value for a given output of an invertible function.
Apply the inverse derivative identity to calculate the slope of an inverse function.
Justify the existence of the inverse derivative by verifying the original derivative is nonzero.
Determine and apply the correct units for the derivative of an inverse function.

sections.title: The Inverse Derivative Identity
sections.content: If a function f is differentiable and has an inverse function g (where g = f⁻¹), the derivative of the inverse at a specific value y₀ is the reciprocal of the derivative of the original function at the corresponding input x₀. Formally, if y₀ = f(x₀), then g'(y₀) = 1 / f'(x₀), provided that f'(x₀) ≠ 0. This relationship exists because the inverse function reflects the original function across the line y = x, which swaps the roles of the independent and dependent variables.

sections.title: The Swap and Reciprocal Strategy
sections.content:
To find the derivative of an inverse function at a point y₀, follow three steps: 1. Point Matching: Find the value x₀ such that f(x₀) = y₀. 2. Verification: Ensure f'(x₀) exists and is not equal to zero. 3. Reciprocal: Calculate the value 1 / f'(x₀). This result is the slope of the inverse function at the point (y₀, x₀).

![A flow chart showing the steps: 1. Identify y0, 2. Find x0 such that f(x0)=y0, 3. Calculate f'(x0), 4. Compute the reciprocal 1/f'(x0).](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/6ce6d442-52d5-4999-8c79-d8835c67f1a6-1786519348578-498.webp)

sections.title: Units and Sign Consistency
sections.content: The units of a derivative represent the ratio of the change in the output to the change in the input (e.g., meters per second). Since an inverse function swaps the roles of input and output, the units of the inverse derivative are the reciprocal of the original units (e.g., seconds per meter). Additionally, the sign of the derivative remains the same: if f is strictly increasing (positive slope), its inverse is also strictly increasing; if f is strictly decreasing (negative slope), its inverse is also strictly decreasing.

worked_examples.question: A differentiable function h(x) represents the volume of water in a tank (liters) at time x (minutes). It is known that h(5) = 12 and h'(5) = 0.4 liters per minute. Find the value of (h⁻¹)'(12) and provide the correct units.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify the point matching. We are asked for the derivative of the inverse at the output y₀ = 12. From the given information, h(5) = 12, so x₀ = 5. Step 2: Verify the derivative at x₀. We are given h'(5) = 0.4. Since 0.4 is not zero, the inverse derivative exists. Step 3: Apply the identity. (h⁻¹)'(12) = 1 / h'(5) = 1 / 0.4. Step 4: Calculate the value. 1 / 0.4 = 2.5. Step 5: Determine units. The original units are liters/minute, so the inverse units are minutes/liter. Final Answer: (h⁻¹)'(12) = 2.5 minutes per liter.

common_mistakes: Using the reciprocal of the output value instead of the reciprocal of the derivative value.
Evaluating the original derivative at y₀ instead of finding the corresponding x₀ first.
Forgetting to flip the units when calculating the rate of change for the inverse function.
Attempting to find the inverse derivative at a point where the original function's slope is zero (where the inverse has a vertical tangent).
exam_tips: Always write out the identity (f⁻¹)'(y₀) = 1 / f'(x₀) to earn justification points.
Double-check the table or graph to ensure you are matching the 'y' value of the original function to the 'x' value of the inverse.
If the derivative of the original function is zero at x₀, state that the derivative of the inverse at y₀ is undefined.
content.recap: The derivative of an inverse function at a point is the reciprocal of the original function's derivative at the corresponding point. To solve, match the inverse's input to the original's output, verify the original derivative is non-zero, and invert both the numerical value and the units.

knowledge_claims.content: The derivative of an inverse function g at point y₀ is given by g'(y₀) = 1 / f'(x₀), where f(x₀) = y₀.
To find the derivative of an inverse at y₀, one must first solve f(x₀) = y₀ to find the corresponding input x₀.
The derivative of an inverse function exists at y₀ only if the original function is differentiable at x₀ and f'(x₀) is not equal to zero.
If a function f is strictly increasing, its inverse function f⁻¹ is also strictly increasing.
If a function f is strictly decreasing, its inverse function f⁻¹ is also strictly decreasing.
The units of the derivative of an inverse function are the reciprocal of the units of the derivative of the original function.
It is a mistake to calculate the inverse derivative by simply taking the reciprocal of the original function's output value.
A vertical tangent line occurs on the graph of an inverse function at y₀ if the derivative of the original function f'(x₀) is zero.
The point (a, b) on the graph of f corresponds to the point (b, a) on the graph of its inverse f⁻¹.
If f'(2) = 3 and f(2) = 5, then the slope of the inverse function at x = 5 is 1/3.
The sign of the derivative of the inverse function (f⁻¹)'(y₀) is always the same as the sign of f'(x₀).
The inverse derivative identity is a specific application of the Chain Rule applied to the equation f(f⁻¹(x)) = x.

items.stem: Which procedure or value is mathematically consistent in “AP Calculus BC — Derivatives of Inverse Functions — Practice Record 01”?

options.A: Derivatives of Inverse Functions: The derivative of an inverse at an output is the reciprocal of the original derivative at the corresponding input when that derivative is nonzero.
options.B: Increasing, Decreasing, and Critical Points: The sign of the first derivative determines intervals of increase and decrease and helps classify local extrema at critical points.
options.C: Integration by Parts and Partial Fractions: Integration by parts reverses the product rule, while partial fractions decomposes rational functions into simpler integrable terms.
options.D: Average Value and Net Change: The average value of a function divides its integral by interval length, while net change integrates a rate with signs preserved.

items.explanation: Choice A is best because The derivative of an inverse at an output is the reciprocal of the original derivative at the corresponding input when that derivative is nonzero. The other options invoke different atomic topics and do not satisfy the record's stated target as directly.

items.stem: Which relationship connects the verbal and symbolic information in “AP Calculus BC — Derivatives of Inverse Functions — Practice Record 02”?

options.A: Concavity and Inflection Points: The sign of the second derivative determines concavity, and an inflection point requires an actual change in concavity.
options.B: Derivatives of Inverse Functions: The derivative of an inverse at an output is the reciprocal of the original derivative at the corresponding input when that derivative is nonzero.
options.C: Improper Integrals: An improper integral is defined by a limit at an infinite bound or unbounded integrand and converges only when that limit is finite.
options.D: Area Between Curves: Area between curves integrates top minus bottom or right minus left after locating relevant intersections and interval changes.
